doc.title: Paul Smith interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 14, 1999

chapter: Dorsey, studios and the changing business
title: Joining Tommy Dorsey and playing for the acts
summary: A call to fill in for Dorsey's fired pianist led to two years playing the band and act music, a good training for sight-reading in studios.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Playing in Lionel Hampton's big band

blocks.x: whether my reading ability, that would be like the first studio work, working on a radio show. That’s what I wanted to do eventually. And we had about a three week break there before we started the show and I went back to San Diego and I got a call from a guy who had been the trombonist way early with Ozzie Nelson, who he was playing trombone for Tommy Dorsey’s band, and he was kind of a road manager. And he called me up and he said, “we’re coming into town next Friday” and he said, “would you like to play one night with the band there?” He said, “Tommy just fired his pianist from Ocean Park up here and he doesn’t have a pianist.” And he said, “I told him about you, and he said get the kid and we’ll give him a shot.” So I said, “gee that’d be fun.” So when the band came down to San Diego I went down sight unseen, hadn’t seen the book or anything. And the first thing the old man did was try to burn me out. I mean in other words he did this kind of a test with all the guys that played solo in the band, like DeFranco and Charlie Shavers and Ziggy and all. So he picked up a tune, the very first tune was a blues thing that Charlie Shavers had written, and it was at a fairly uptempo from his standpoint, it was like a ballad to me, having played with Les. And he would do this at you, five choruses. Okay. He played five choruses. Ten more. You played ten more. And he’d have you play 30, 40 choruses. And most guys after about ten choruses at about this tempo [claps], they begin to slow down. And I’d been doing that, I could do that with one hand. Because that was a ballad tempo with Les. So when they ended the first set, the trombone, Wes Cope was his name, he came over and he said, “the old man wants to know if you want to join the band.” And I thought this would be a great experience because he was playing a lot of vaudeville shows at the time. Like when the band would go out it would be Tommy Dorsey and his Orchestra featuring such-and-such dancers, the Step Brothers, we played with them. And you’ve got to read their music.
In addition to playing with Dorsey, you’ve got to play the other people’s music.

Yeah, you play the whole show. It’s an hour show, mainly featuring the band, but the band would play an opener and maybe one tune that was familiar to them “Well Get It” or something, and then you go into your acts. And there’s a whole variety of acts you have to play and a lot of their music is written on papyrus and it’s also written in blue chalk, you know, it’s terrible stuff to read. But it’s great experience. It’s the best experience I had. And I stayed with them in ’47 and ’48, two years, reading all this funny stuff. So I felt I would be more capable when I came back to L.A. to do some studio work, which is immediate sight reading. I mean that’s why it’s a closed corporation. I mean you walk in there at nine o’clock in the morning and there it is, and you play it once to make sure the copyist didn’t make any mistakes, and then you record, and that’s it.
